paras: The Hardeeville bridge hands shooting was the killing of a Black laborer by a white mechanic from Baltimore at the railroad station in Hardeeville, South Carolina, on the night of Saturday, May 27, 1882. The shooting was reported as self-defense, and the papers gave most attention to what followed, when Black workers tried to seize the white men and, in the wire's words, "attempted to lynch the killer, but were prevented."

A gang of skilled mechanics from Baltimore had been sent to put in place a new iron railroad bridge over the Savannah River, about seven or eight miles from Hardeeville, alongside a large gang of Black laborers. According to the Savannah Morning News, some of the Black workers had lately been "subordinate and turbulent" and, refused the use of the only hand car, took it anyway to go up to Hardeeville on Saturday. Two of the white mechanics went to Hardeeville that afternoon for their mail and reprimanded the workers, many of whom the paper said had been drinking, for taking the car.

The paper's account, from D. S. Leslie of Charleston, a passenger on the belated evening train, held that the workers later tried to assault the two white men as they pushed through a crowd to reach the cars, and that one of the white men drew a pistol "in self-defense" and fired, killing a Black man. Leslie heard two shots, after which the two men ran along the platform pursued by Black men he estimated at about two hundred, armed with bludgeons, pistols and a gun, who "swore they would have the lives of the white men."

The white men hid in the smoking car, and the crowd, told they had jumped off the other side, lost their trail. The passenger cars were found uncoupled, which the paper presumed the workers had done, and a few passengers kept the crowd from entering the cars while shots were fired and the search went on for more than fifteen minutes. Once the train left, the two white men were found aboard and rode on to Savannah.

The Savannah paper could not learn the names of the dead man or the two white men and said an inquest would be held at Hardeeville the next day. No report of the inquest's finding, an arrest or a trial appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News ran the fullest account under the headline "Homicide at Hardeeville. Trouble Among the Bridge Hands—A Negro Killed—Intense Excitement and Threats of Lynching," telling it from the white men's and passengers' side and calling the workers' conduct "exceedingly violent and boisterous." A one-sentence wire brief ran the same day in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, the Wilmington Daily Gazette and the Daily Republican, hedging the self-defense claim with "it is alleged." Washington's National Republican identified the shooter as "a white man from Baltimore," as did the Savannah dispatch printed in the Dallas Daily Herald on May 30 and weeklies in Maryland and Arkansas into June, while the Daily Globe placed the town in Georgia and stated self-defense without qualification. No Black-press coverage survives from this period, and no account from the Black workers' side was found.
The Daily Globe put Hardeeville in Georgia, probably from the Savannah dateline, while the other briefs place it in South Carolina.

bases: A Black laborer was shot dead by one white man in a quarrel among bridge workers, after which a crowd of Black workers tried to seize and kill the white men; no group killed anyone (A2, A5, A6).

The only death was a Black man shot by a single white man, reported as self-defense (A2, A6); the 'attempt to lynch' was by a Black crowd against the white men, who escaped unharmed on the train (A2, A6).
The wire briefs (A1, A2, A5) and the local account (A6) all appear to originate in Savannah on the same night, and A6 rests on one passenger's report; no independent second account was found.

accounts.gist: Black workers who had taken a hand car against orders and been drinking quarreled with and then tried to assault the two white men; when the white men tried to reach the train, one fired in self-defense; about two hundred Black men then hunted them on the train, which they escaped on.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A colored man was killed by a white man, 'it is alleged, in self-defense', in a fight among bridge builders; the negroes attempted to lynch the killer but were prevented.

framing.detail: Northern dailies ran a one-sentence brief in news summaries, presenting the killing as self-defense and the Black workers' pursuit as an attempted lynching.

The Savannah Morning News ('Homicide at Hardeeville... Threats of Lynching') adopted the white side's account, describing the Black workers as 'subordinate [insubordinate] and turbulent', drunk and 'exceedingly violent'.

conflicts.note: Two briefs say South Carolina; the Daily Globe's 'Ga.' likely comes from the Savannah dateline.
All versions come from the white side; no Black account or inquest finding was found.
